In my opinion, one of easiest way to reduce your daily CO2 footprint is by going by bike or public transportation to university/sports/etc. instead of your own car/motorcycle. Taking the bike, besides doing something for the climate, also helps you stay healthy.

Additionally, reducing and recycling waste is important. Reducing waste can be easily done by using your own re-usable shopping bag (instead getting a new plastic bag every time) and bringing your own Tupperware if you get food to-go. TooGoodToGo is an app that helps reduce food waste of restaurants and you get a cheap and good meal. Recycling waste helps not only the environment but also saves you money in Zurich, since the blue bag costs money but bringing your glass/aluminium/paper to a "Werkstoffhof" is free.

A third way to help the environment is eating less meat. I, myself, am not a vegetarian but I have reduced my meat intake to once a week maximum. Animals need water and food and growing this food needs space. Often soja plants are used, which are planted in the South American rainforest, killing the living space for a lot of animals and decreasing the amount of trees that can convert CO2 to O2 via photosynthesis.

In Zurich, students can do a lot to fight climate change without making it too complicated. For starters, it's easy to cut down on energy use: switching to LEDs, using energy-efficient devices, and turning things off when you're not using them. If the electricity comes from renewable sources, that's even better!
When it comes to getting around, Zurich's public transport is great, so hopping on a tram or bus instead of driving makes a big difference. If biking is an option thats even better. It's good for both the planet and your health. For those who do need to drive, carpooling or choosing an electric vehicle can help reduce emissions.
Eating habits matter too. Cutting back on meat, especially red meat, helps a lot because the meat industry has a huge carbon footprint. Supporting local, seasonal, and organic food alos reduces emissions form transporting food. And of course, recycling, composting and avoiding single-use plastics are simple but effective ways to reduce waste.
Students can also spread awareness by talking about climate change and sharing tips on sustainable living. Whether it's through discussions, workshops, or just chatting with friends, the more people who know about it, the better. Supporting sustainable businesses is another way to make an impact.
Lastly, getting involved in university sustainability projects is also a great way to actively contribute. UZH has programs aimed at reducing their environmental footprint, and students can join in or eve start their own initiatives. Advocating for policies that promote sustainability on campus or in the local community is another powerful way to make a change.
By making some of these small changes and encouraging others to do the same, students in Zurich can definitely be part of the solution to climate change.

Each of us can do many different things to help combat climate change to some degree. While many people making small changes in their everyday lives can make a difference too, I think it is far more important, that we become conscious of the main culprits, which are for example most huge corporations (and not you or me taking an airplane once a year).

These are horrific contributors to not only the destruction of our planet, but also the exploitation of workers, not to speak of the toxicity of the chemicals in their unregulated products. People claiming to care even a bit about the environment, while shopping on such platforms, are extremely hypocritical. And seeing how 96% believe climate change to be an important topic, while Temu sales are only rising further, I would say that includes a pretty big part of those people as well. 
But not only these online platforms are a problem. Most clothing retailers for example, have massively lowered the quality of their products over the last few years, while going for more and more mass production. Microplastic for example has been a huge concern for quite some time and it is only getting worse, with even the majority of clothes being made out of plastic nowadays. 
So my appeal to all fellow students would be to stop supporting corporations like Temu, Shien, etc. and try to steer away from unnecessary mass consumption of low quality mass produced products altogether.

By adjusting our consumption we also have a powerful lever to influence these large global firms that are among the main polluters, by reducing demand for their products and requesting accountability and responsibility for harm towards the environment on a political alley. We can collectively cast repeated votes not only in the political arena, but also in everyday choices. Concretely, I would suggest drastically reducing the amount of flights individuals take per year, especially short flights that could easily be done by train or bus, reducing the amount of meat and animal products individuals consume, as they are among the largest causes for CO2 emissions. Just switching from factory farming to more "humane" sources is not a fix, as they are about increasing well being, not reducing environmental impact. If it is possible for you to cut out meat and other animal products entirely, that is the way to go from an environmentalist perspective, but also from an animal ethics perspective. If not, reduce, and choose good sources, avoid factory farming at all costs. Finally, other consumption habits can also have an important impact, for example if you order online less frequently, in general buy less stuff, because stuff needs to be manufactured and shipped around the world, and also take care of what you own. Don't treat things with less care because they are cheap and readily available, always try to maximize the lifespan of anything you buy. Maybe choose better quality products from the get-go, if your budget allows it, that you never even have to face the sentiment of "Oh, this was cheap, it doesn't really matter if it breaks". Also avoid going into sales looking for bargains to be made, like is common on promotional campaigns such as black friday. Buy what you need, not what is currently cheaper than usually. Generally, I feel most have a good understanding of what is good and what is bad for the environment, the question is more about who should bare the responsibility. I don't think it's helpful to shift it either way, but rather to focus on maximized sustainability from everyone. If the world becomes uninhabitable, no one cares about I told you so, so let's make sure we can avoid an uninhabitable world.

As (probably somewhat affluent) people living in central europe, we'll be among the ones least affected by climate change. Still our outlook doesn't look good. And as if that wasn't enough: the outlook for the next couple of generations looks even worse.
Climate change is one of the main examples for how the normality we inhabit is in many ways unacceptable. How the life we're used to is currently tied to a huge amount of present, past and future suffering and destruction. This is not a happy thought.

Shortly after the US-elections of 2024, the CEO of Partners In Health wrote in their newsletter about hopelessness and staying motivated to try to better things. She said that PIH feels as motivated as ever because they know the following two things to be true:
1. "Action is the antidote to despair."
2. "Bending the arc toward justice forbids us the luxury of being pessimistic on behalf of those who can't afford to loose hope."
I quite like this because it shows two facets of altruism. 1. A sense of empowerment. 2. A sense of responsibility (in the 'duty' sense, not in the 'blame' sense). To me this is motivating.

Yet, we are students. And as such, don't we usually lack the time and money to spend on good causes? There are all the everyday choices we make that strongly influence our personal contribution to the problem (what do I eat, what transportation do I use, how much do I buy) and there are the votes we cast. And all these things are already something. We can 'do our part'. But a lingering feeling remains that this won't solve the problem; at no time will everybody be doing their part and not at all times will we be doing our part. Luckily there is more we can do:
- Since the Swiss currency is so strong, I think we should not underestimate the impact our donations can have. What looks like a small sum to us might look larger in another country.
- As students we are still very much in the process of choosing the skills we want to acquire, the field we want to work in etc. All these choices might not really have any impact on the external world right now, but they could have a huge impact on the influence we have on the world over the course of our lives.
- Maybe we can already get a little more involved in politics after all. We don't need to be Nationalrat to collect signatures or do campaigning.

One of the most immediate ways we can act is by rethinking our transport habits. In Zurich, we are fortunate to have a highly efficient public transportation system. Choosing trams, buses, or bikes instead of cars helps cut emissions significantly. Walking or cycling to university not only reduces carbon output but also improves health, sometimes it's faster too. 
Another important step is reducing energy consumption. As engineering students, we can apply our technical knowledge to make smarter choices; whether that means using energy-efficient appliances in our apartments or developing low-power systems as part of our academic projects. In fact, we can even integrate sustainability into our coursework and research by focusing on renewable energy, power efficiency, and sustainable design.
Food choices also matter. Eating less meat and choosing local, seasonal produce reduces the carbon footprint of our diets. In Zurich, many stores and markets support sustainable shopping, making it easier to make conscious decisions. 
Each small step contributes to a larger shift. As engineering students, we have not just the responsibility but also the tools to help design a sustainable future.

On an individual level, I think there are several domains in which our choices can have a tangible effect on combating climate change, especially if these choices are adopted by the general population and not just a handful of people.

The first, and the likely easiest domain where one can make a difference in Switzerland, is the consumer behaviour. This includes things like adjusting behaviour related to fashion, food, transport etc. For instance, instead of supporting a polluting fashion industry with opaque supply chains and dubious labour practices, we could buy second hand clothes, or clothes manufactured ethically from Europe. Similarly, buying local produce that is in season rather than produce shipped from the other corner of the globe while also avoiding food waste is not only healthy but also good for the environment. For transport, opting for trains and public transport rather (at least in Europe) than planes and cars would also be a good step forward. 

Another domain that I think is important to consider in order to combat climate change is politics. While it is true that individuals should be aware of their consumer behaviour, it is also well known that private companies are by far the largest pollutors. In my opinion, companies should be held accountable for their emissions and general environmental impact. Currently, due to an inconsistent set of regulations with loopholes, grey areas and ambiguous requirements (not only in Switzerland but also the EU), many companies are likely not doing enough to combat climate change. As consumers but also as citizens, we have the right to require our politicians to pass laws that regulate the activities of companies such that their impact on the environment is either offset through taxes or through social programs. Luckily in Switzerland, citizen invoked referendums have a lot of weight on decision making which is why getting involved in groups or organizations that promote the regularization of companies and in general the fight against climate change is in my opinion more effective than individual action. 

Additional to the point made above, while individual consumer choices can help to an extent (and are by far the most comfortable way of contributing and feeling good about yourself for tackling climate change), being socially involved is probably the most important contribution you can have. In my opinion, the individualistic convenience culture that we live in has the insidious side effect that it makes people think that climate change is also a matter of individual action, conveniently fixable by only adjusting our consumer practices. In reality, at least in my opinion, climate change was never an individual isssue and it cannot be fixed by individuals, it can only by fixed with social inititiatives and with the engagement of communities.

Post:
I believe that each one of us needs to be more aware of the use of any tool, technological or otherwise, in order to better understand the impact it can have in the long term and added to the population as whole. At this time in history, scientific development is stronger than ever, but the continuous desire to improve our lives only makes future lives worse and worse. Climate change is an issue that may not affect us during our individual lifetimes, but could heavily influence the lives of those who will follow us. 

I am in favour of progress, but I am even more in favour of the conscientious use of the means we have at our disposal, so that each of us can assess whether it is worth it or not. My advice is to think about this not by seeing ourselves as individuals in out own right, but as part of a world and a species that cannot move forward if everyone continues to think only of their own good. 

I am not the kind of person who would demonstrate in the streets to hope for a revolution in a specific area, such as climate change; I am the kind of person who would focus on raising the individual's awareness and developing critical and ethical thinking, which does not only think of the good of oneself, but of all living beings indiscriminately. And only in this way could we truly hope to change something.
